doc.title: Art Farmer — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Tyner, Coltrane and Giant Steps
summary: Meeting Trane in Los Angeles, his later achievement, and Farmer's feeling that Giant Steps was beyond him.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: By the time the Jazztet had folded, McCoy had already spent a considerable period with John Coltrane, who was now starting to pioneer a new sound, or at least to expand his creative language. Did you talk to McCoy later?
Not in any detail. We would run into each other sometime, – what are you doing, how are you feeling, what’s going on? – but nothing more pointed than that. We never talked about the music.
What was your opinion or impression when all of a sudden John Coltrane starts to expand his…

When I first met Trane, he came out to Los Angeles with a group that Dizzy had put together. It was Trane and Jimmy Heath on the saxophone, Percy Heath was playing bass, Specs Wright from Philadelphia was playing drums, and Milt Jackson was in the group. They didn’t have a pianist, so everybody took turns playing the piano. I met Trane then, and that’s the first time I heard him play. He sounded fine, but to me, he was just another young guy like everybody else trying to get it together. By the time he organized his group with Elvin Jones and Tyner, he had it together then. At least, he sounded like he had it together to me because he was doing things in such a way that they had not been done before, not even by Charlie Parker.
Even before McCoy Tyner joined the group, John Coltrane had recorded Giant Steps. Did that have an impact on you? Do you recall hearing that for the first time?
It had an impact on me in so much that I felt that it was out of my realm of possibility.
Even after working with George Russell and all of the other things you had been doing?

Yeah! It was harder than George Russell--to improvise. I have to tell you, the joke about Giant Steps was that there used to be a great saxophone player and writer around New York named Al Cohn, and the story goes that somebody asked on a gig, “Al,
do you play ‘Giant Steps.’” He said, “Yes, I play ‘Giant Steps’ with my own changes” [laughs]. The changes in “Giant Steps” separates the players from the would be.
